headline: Student Survey Transformed NYC School Lunches
meta_description: A Brooklyn high school student's survey led to cafeteria redesigns across NYC, raising lunch participation by 35% and showing how youth advocacy creates real c…
summary_short: Leslie Gomez Rivera's survey at Midwood High School in Brooklyn sparked a citywide movement that redesigned over 200 cafeterias and increased lunch participation by 35%.
body:
When Leslie Gomez Rivera surveyed roughly 100 students at Midwood High School in Brooklyn, she wasn't just gathering opinions—she was starting a movement that would reshape school lunch across New York City. The 16-year-old, working with Youth Food Advocates (YFA), discovered that students actually liked popcorn chicken, sauces, fruit, and salads; they wanted more food from home; and they avoided the cafeteria not because food was bad, but because it felt hectic and carried a social stigma. Armed with this organized feedback, Rivera met with her cafeteria manager and principal, who were receptive to her findings. She then worked with student leadership to promote the redesigned space, helping bring participation back to full capacity—a pivotal achievement that taught her a crucial lesson: "If you want it done, you can do it yourself."

Her work became a blueprint for change. YFA students developed a toolkit for schools rolling out redesigned cafeterias, recommending deli-style stations, comfortable seating, and queuing systems that cut wait times. By December 2025, more than 200 cafeterias had been renovated using these insights. The results speak clearly: lunch participation rose 35 percent at redesigned high schools, according to city data analysis.

What makes this story remarkable isn't just the numbers—it's what happened next. Rivera's younger siblings later attended Midwood and enjoyed the enhanced cafeteria. She went on to work with Green Guerillas teaching civic engagement, and has testified at city budget hearings. Now 22, she represents something powerful: young people who discovered their voices matter. Experts note that students, eating lunch daily, are uniquely positioned to identify problems others miss. That perspective, channeled into collaborative conversations with cafeteria staff rather than blame, created lasting change that benefits not just this generation but all students to come.
quick_facts: Leslie Gomez Rivera surveyed 100 Midwood High students in Brooklyn
Over 200 NYC cafeterias redesigned using student-developed toolkit
Lunch participation increased 35% at redesigned high schools
YFA trains NYC students to research and advocate for food policy changes
